message.content:
The lion (Panthera leo) and the zebra (Equus quagga) are both placental mammals, but they belong to two different orders: **Carnivora** for the lion and **Perissodactyla** for the zebra.  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore a member of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**, the group that gave rise to many of the modern “placental” mammals that evolved on the northern continents after the breakup of Pangaea.

**Key points**

| Lineage | Order | Divergence from the other lineage |
|---------|-------|-----------------------------------|
| Lion | Carnivora | Split from the perissodactyl lineage ~55–60 million years ago (Paleocene) |
| Zebra | Perissodactyla | Split from the carnivoran lineage ~55–60 million years ago (Paleocene) |

So the common ancestor of lion and zebra was a small, early mammal that lived roughly 55–60 million years ago, before the two lineages diverged into the distinct orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. It would have been a relatively generalized, probably insectivorous or omnivorous mammal, not a recognizable modern species.
